A Christmas Carol. When this novella was published in 1843, it became Charles Dickens's story of spiritual redemption. At its heart is Ebenezer Scrooge, a wealthy businessman who dismisses Christmas with the famous words "Bah, humbug!" and shows no concern for those who suffer. On Christmas Eve, he's visited by the ghost of Jacob Marley, his dead business partner, followed by three more spirits: the Ghost of Christmas Past, the Ghost of Christmas Present, and the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come. Through these visits, Scrooge is forced to witness moments from his own life and to see the consequences of his actions. He sees the happiness he's denied to others, and he's shown the hollow, unmourned death waiting for him. Central to the story is Tiny Tim, the sickly but cheerful son of Bob Cratchit, Scrooge's clerk. This innocent child becomes the moral center of the entire tale. By the story's end, Scrooge undergoes a complete transformation. He becomes generous and warm-hearted, adopts Tiny Tim, and finds redemption through his sudden awareness of his own mortality. The novella was so powerful that it essentially created the modern ghost story as a literary genre, and it became the most adapted literary work of the entire nineteenth century. Its message of charity, social responsibility, and the possibility of personal change shaped how we think about Christmas to this day.
